beats.text: He knew exactly what he was stopping.
beats.note: Marcus Hutchins says on his own blog that he registered the domain as a routine sinkhole. He still did not know much about what it was for.

beats.text: The malware asked if a web address existed.
beats.note: If the unregistered domain could not be reached, it encrypted files. Once it was registered, spread halted at 15:03 UTC on 12 May 2017, according to Wikipedia. Machines already infected stayed locked.

beats.context: Between Microsoft's MS17-010 patch on 14 March 2017 and the attack on 12 May. Wikipedia says patches existed for all then supported versions of Windows.

beats.text: The exploit was reportedly the NSA's.
beats.note: Wikipedia says EternalBlue was developed by the US National Security Agency and was likely stolen from it. The Shadow Brokers published it about a month before the attack.

beats.text: At least 81 of 236 trusts were hit.
beats.note: The National Audit Office identified 6,912 cancelled appointments, and NHS England estimated over 19,000 in total. Five A&E departments diverted patients. No NHS organisation paid the ransom.

beats.text: He now doubts it was a kill switch.
beats.note: Hutchins later wrote that he believes it was a badly thought out anti-analysis check. Sandboxes answer every lookup, so the malware would exit when the domain seemed to resolve.

beats.text: One routine registration slowed a global attack.
